title: Postgres Indexes: The Field Handbook
summary: A dense, practical tour of PostgreSQL indexing — how btree, hash, GIN, GiST, and BRIN actually work inside, when each wins, and how partial, expression, and covering indexes plus index-only scans turn a slow query into a fast one.

chapters.title: Access Paths & Why Indexes Exist
points: Heap = unordered pages of 8 KB; a seq scan reads every page regardless of WHERE selectivity
Index = separate data structure mapping key values to TIDs (ctid = block number + item offset)
Postgres indexes are secondary indexes only — there is no clustered/primary-storage index like InnoDB
Access path types: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan
Bitmap scan builds a TID bitmap, sorts it, then reads the heap in physical order — good for medium selectivity and for combining multiple indexes with AND/OR
Planner picks by estimated cost, not by rules: cost = seq_page_cost(1.0) + random_page_cost(4.0) + cpu_tuple_cost(0.01) + cpu_index_tuple_cost(0.005) + cpu_operator_cost(0.0025)
Selectivity comes from pg_statistic via ANALYZE: n_distinct, most_common_vals/freqs, histogram_bounds, correlation
Rule of thumb: index wins under roughly 5-10% row selectivity; above that, seq scan is cheaper because random I/O dominates
On SSD set random_page_cost = 1.1 — the 4.0 default assumes spinning disks and suppresses index use
Index costs writes: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must maintain every index on the table
Read `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` — compare `rows=` estimated vs actual; a 100x gap means bad stats, not a bad index
`Rows Removed by Filter` in EXPLAIN means the index fetched rows the WHERE clause then threw away — the index is not selective enough
Index Cond (evaluated inside the index) vs Filter (evaluated after heap fetch) — moving a predicate from Filter to Index Cond is the core optimization
Every table has one implicit index per PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint; FOREIGN KEY columns get none, a classic source of slow cascading deletes

chapters.title: B-tree Internals
points: Default index type; balanced multi-way tree, all leaves at the same depth, typically 3-4 levels for hundreds of millions of rows
Structure: meta page, root, internal pages holding separator keys + downlinks, leaf pages holding (key, TID) tuples in sorted order
Fanout ~ page_size / entry_size; with 8 KB pages a 3-level tree addresses billions of keys, so lookup is ~4 page reads
Complexity: search O(log n), insert O(log n), range scan O(log n + k) for k matched rows
Leaf pages are doubly linked left-to-right (Lehman & Yao B-link tree), so range scans and backward scans walk siblings without revisiting the root
B-link right-links allow concurrent readers to proceed during a page split without holding tree-wide locks
Page split: full page splits ~50/50, or 90/10 when inserting at the rightmost edge (monotonic keys like serial/now())
fillfactor default 90 for btree — leaves 10% free space for HOT-friendly growth; lower it for heavily updated indexes
Deduplication (PG 13+): repeated keys stored once as a posting list of TIDs, shrinking low-cardinality indexes dramatically
Bottom-up index deletion (PG 14+) reclaims dead entries before splitting a page, fighting version churn bloat from non-HOT updates
Index tuples have no visibility info — they carry no xmin/xmax, which is why the heap or visibility map must be consulted
Index entries exist for dead tuples too; only VACUUM removes them
Supports operators < <= = >= > , BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, and LIKE 'prefix%' (only with C collation or a text_pattern_ops index)
Provides ordered output for free: ORDER BY on the index key can skip the sort node entirely
Max index entry size ~2704 bytes (1/3 page) — indexing long text throws `index row size exceeds maximum`; hash the value or use an expression index instead

chapters.title: B-tree in Practice: Multicolumn, Order, Sorting
points: Multicolumn index keys are compared left-to-right, so only a leftmost prefix of columns can be used as an Index Cond
`CREATE INDEX ON t (a, b, c)` serves WHERE a=?, (a=?, b=?), (a=?, b=?, c=?) — but NOT WHERE b=? alone
Equality columns first, range column last: for `WHERE a = 1 AND b > 5 ORDER BY c`, index (a, b) stops the scan at b; index (a, c) also gives free sort — measure both
A range predicate ends usable index ordering: everything after the first inequality column becomes a filter, not a bound
Column order does not matter for a pure bitmap AND of two separate single-column indexes, but a composite is nearly always faster
Per-column sort direction: `CREATE INDEX ON t (a DESC, b ASC)` — needed for mixed-direction ORDER BY to avoid a Sort node
NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST must match the query's ORDER BY for the index to satisfy it; default is NULLS LAST for ASC, NULLS FIRST for DESC
B-tree indexes DO store NULLs (unlike Oracle), so `WHERE col IS NULL` can use an index scan
Keyset pagination `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20` uses a (created_at, id) index; OFFSET 100000 does not
Row-comparison syntax `(a, b) > (1, 2)` maps directly to a composite index bound; the expanded OR form usually does not
Operator classes: text_pattern_ops / varchar_pattern_ops enable LIKE 'abc%' under non-C collations; `COLLATE "C"` on the column achieves the same
Changing lc_collate (e.g. a glibc upgrade) silently corrupts text btree ordering — REINDEX after any collation version change
Index on (a) is redundant if index on (a, b) exists — drop the narrow one unless it is much smaller and hot
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` enforces uniqueness; NULLs are distinct by default, use `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+) to forbid multiple NULLs

chapters.title: Hash Indexes
points: `CREATE INDEX ... USING hash (col)` — supports exactly one operator: equality (=)
Stores a 32-bit hash code of the value, not the value itself, so index size is independent of the column's data width
Structure: meta page + buckets; each bucket is a primary page plus an overflow page chain; bitmap pages track free overflow pages
Lookup is O(1) expected — hash the key, jump to the bucket, scan the bucket page
Bucket splits happen incrementally as the index grows, not as a single giant rehash
Before PG 10 hash indexes were NOT WAL-logged: unsafe on crash, not replicated. PG 10+ made them crash-safe and replicable
Real win: indexing very long values (URLs, long text keys) where a btree entry would be huge or exceed the size limit
Cannot support ORDER BY, range queries, LIKE, uniqueness constraints, primary keys, or exclusion constraints
Cannot be multicolumn — one column only
Cannot be used for index-only scans: the original value is not recoverable from the hash
Hash collisions are possible, so Postgres always rechecks the actual value against the heap tuple
Practical verdict: btree on the same column is usually within a few percent and far more flexible — reach for hash only on wide equality-only keys
Alternative that works everywhere: a btree expression index on `md5(long_col)` or `hashtext(long_col)` with a matching query predicate

chapters.title: GIN: Inverted Index for Composite Values
points: GIN = Generalized Inverted Index — for column types holding many elements: arrays, jsonb, tsvector, trigrams
Structure: a btree over extracted keys (the distinct elements); each key points to a posting list (small) or a posting tree (large, its own btree of TIDs)
Answers 'which rows contain this element' — the exact inverse of btree's 'which rows equal this value'
Full-text search: `CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body))` serves the `@@` match operator
jsonb default operator class jsonb_ops indexes every key AND every value; supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&
jsonb_path_ops indexes hashes of whole key→value paths: much smaller and faster, but supports only @> containment
Arrays: `WHERE tags @> ARRAY['pg']` and `&&` (overlap) are GIN-accelerated
pg_trgm extension + `USING gin (col gin_trgm_ops)` makes arbitrary `LIKE '%substring%'` and `ILIKE` indexable, plus fuzzy `%` similarity
Writes are slow because one row touches many index keys; the `fastupdate` pending list buffers inserts and flushes them in batches
Consequence of fastupdate: an occasional query pays the flush cost, and a big pending list must be scanned linearly — tune `gin_pending_list_limit` (default 4 MB)
`gin_fuzzy_search_limit` caps rows returned from very common search terms
GIN is lossy in the sense that results always require a recheck against the heap — no index-only scans
Not for range queries or sorting; use for containment, overlap, and text search only
Build cost tip: raise `maintenance_work_mem` before a large GIN build; it dominates build speed

chapters.title: GiST and SP-GiST: Extensible Trees
points: GiST = Generalized Search Tree — a balanced tree framework where the data type supplies consistent, union, penalty, picksplit, and same methods
Internal nodes store a lossy summary (bounding box / predicate) of their subtree, so a search descends every branch whose summary might match
Lossy summaries mean GiST results are approximate: every candidate row is rechecked against the heap
Unlike btree, GiST subtree regions may overlap — search can follow multiple paths, making worst-case performance data-dependent
Geometric & spatial: PostGIS `geometry` uses GiST for &&, <->, ST_Intersects bounding-box filtering
Range types: `USING gist (period)` accelerates @>, &&, <<, >> on tstzrange/int4range
Exclusion constraints are GiST's killer feature: `EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)` prevents double-booking — impossible with btree
btree_gist extension lets scalar types join a GiST index so equality columns can sit beside a range column in one exclusion constraint
K-nearest-neighbour: `ORDER BY point <-> '(0,0)' LIMIT 10` is answered directly by an ordered GiST scan, no full sort
pg_trgm also offers gist_trgm_ops — smaller and faster to build than GIN, but slower to search; GIN wins for read-heavy text search
GiST updates are cheaper than GIN's; prefer GiST when the column is written often
SP-GiST = Space-Partitioned GiST: unbalanced, non-overlapping partitions — quadtrees, k-d trees, radix tries
SP-GiST excels at point data, IP addresses (inet), and text prefix search where partitions never overlap
Rough comparison row: GIN = fast search / slow build / big; GiST = medium search / fast build / small / supports KNN and exclusion

chapters.title: BRIN: Block Range Indexes
points: BRIN = Block Range INdex — stores a summary (min/max) per range of heap blocks instead of one entry per row
`pages_per_range` defaults to 128, so one index tuple summarizes 1 MB of heap — index size is tiny, often thousands of times smaller than btree
Scan method: read summaries, discard ranges whose min/max cannot match, then scan the surviving heap blocks and recheck every tuple — always a bitmap heap scan
Lossy by design: BRIN never proves a row matches, only that a block range might
Only useful when physical row order correlates with the indexed column — check `correlation` in pg_stats, want > 0.9 or < -0.9
Canonical fit: append-only time-series with a created_at/timestamp column, or a log table with a monotonically increasing id
Anti-pattern: BRIN on a randomly distributed column (uuid, hashed key) — every range matches, degenerating into a seq scan plus overhead
Trade-off: ~1000x smaller and far cheaper to maintain than btree, but much less precise and useless for point lookups on scattered data
Lower pages_per_range = more precision + bigger index; raise it for very large, very well-correlated tables
New ranges are summarized on VACUUM or by `brin_summarize_new_values('idx')`; `autosummarize = on` handles it automatically
PG 14+ multi-minmax opclass (`int8_minmax_multi_ops`) stores several intervals per range, tolerating outliers that would otherwise widen a summary to uselessness
PG 14+ bloom opclass (`int8_bloom_ops`) makes BRIN handle equality on uncorrelated data via a per-range bloom filter
CLUSTER on a btree index physically reorders the table and can create the correlation BRIN needs — but it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and does not stay clustered
BRIN supports no sorting, no uniqueness, no index-only scans

chapters.title: Partial and Expression Indexes
points: Partial index: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` — indexes only the rows matching the predicate
Why it wins: smaller index, faster scans, less write amplification, and the excluded rows cost nothing on INSERT/UPDATE
Classic pattern: index the tiny hot slice of a huge table (unprocessed jobs, soft-deleted = false, active subscriptions)
The planner must PROVE the query predicate implies the index predicate — `WHERE status = 'pending'` matches, `WHERE status = $1` with a parameter does not
Proof is syntactic and limited: keep the index WHERE clause simple and repeat it literally in queries
Partial unique index enforces conditional uniqueness: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` — one live email, many deleted ones
`WHERE col IS NOT NULL` on a mostly-NULL column can shrink an index by orders of magnitude at zero query cost
Expression index: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` — only used if the query writes exactly `WHERE lower(email) = ...`, never `WHERE email = ...`
Any function used in an expression index must be IMMUTABLE — `now()`, `current_date`, and unqualified casts of timestamptz→date are not
Common expression indexes: `(date_trunc('day', ts))`, `((data->>'user_id'))`, `(col::text)`, `(a + b)`, `(md5(long_text))`
Expression indexes make the planner collect separate statistics on the expression's result — sometimes worth creating just for the better estimates
The two combine freely: `CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload->>'type')) WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'`
Cost: expression indexes evaluate the function on every insert and update of the row
Alternative for case-insensitive matching: the citext type, or a generated column plus an ordinary index (PG 12+)

chapters.title: Index-Only Scans, Covering Indexes, Visibility
points: Index-only scan returns all needed columns straight from the index, skipping the heap entirely — the single biggest available speedup for wide tables
Requirement 1: every column referenced anywhere in the query (SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY) must be in the index
Requirement 2: the heap page must be marked all-visible in the visibility map, because index tuples carry no MVCC visibility info
Visibility map = 2 bits per heap page (all-visible, all-frozen); only VACUUM sets the bits, and any write clears them
So an index-only scan on a freshly written table still hits the heap — run VACUUM (or wait for autovacuum) and re-measure
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows `Heap Fetches: N` — N near 0 means a true index-only scan, N near rows means the visibility map is stale
INCLUDE columns (PG 11+): `CREATE INDEX ON t (a) INCLUDE (b, c)` stores b and c in leaf pages only — not searchable, not sortable, but available for index-only scans
INCLUDE vs adding the column to the key: INCLUDE keeps internal pages small, permits non-btree-indexable types, and lets a UNIQUE index cover extra columns without widening the constraint
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON t (email) INCLUDE (name)` keeps the uniqueness on email alone while covering name
count(*) over a range can go index-only, which is why a narrow covering index beats a seq scan for dashboard counters
Index-only scans are supported by btree, GiST (for some opclasses), and SP-GiST — never by GIN, hash, or BRIN
Trade-off: covering indexes are wider, so fewer entries per page, bigger index, slower writes — do not blindly INCLUDE every selected column
Aggressive tuning: lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` on the table to keep the visibility map fresh for index-only scans
Anti-pattern: `SELECT *` guarantees no index-only scan; list the columns you actually need

chapters.title: Maintenance, Mistakes, and Choosing
points: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoids the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock: two table passes, cannot run in a transaction block, and leaves an INVALID index if it fails
Recover from a failed concurrent build: find it via `pg_index.indisvalid = false`, then `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and retry
`REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` (PG 12+) rebuilds a bloated index online; `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` removes one without blocking readers
Index bloat comes from MVCC: UPDATE writes a new row version and a new index entry for every non-HOT-updated index
HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) update skips index maintenance entirely — but only if no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same page (leave room via fillfactor)
Find unused indexes: `SELECT relname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0` — check across a full business cycle before dropping
Measure size with `pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx'))`; use pgstattuple or pg_stat_user_indexes to estimate bloat
Common mistake: wrapping the column in a function — `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01'` kills the index; use a range `>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2026-01-02'`
Common mistake: implicit type mismatch — an int column compared to a text parameter, or varchar vs text under different collations, disables the index
Common mistake: leading wildcard `LIKE '%foo'` on a btree — needs pg_trgm GIN instead
Common mistake: indexing a low-cardinality boolean; use a partial index on the rare value instead
Common mistake: OR across columns forces a bitmap OR or seq scan — rewrite as UNION ALL or add a matching composite/expression index
Common mistake: too many indexes on a write-heavy table — each one is a synchronous write plus WAL on every row change
Stale statistics beat every index: run ANALYZE after bulk loads, and raise `default_statistics_target` (default 100) for skewed columns

Chooser summary — equality on scalars: btree; equality on huge values: hash; containment/text search/jsonb/arrays: GIN; ranges, geometry, KNN, exclusion constraints: GiST; prefix/point/IP partitioning: SP-GiST; huge correlated append-only tables: BRIN

Workflow to internalize: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) → check estimate vs actual → move Filter into Index Cond → verify Heap Fetches → confirm the index is actually used in production via pg_stat_user_indexes
